title: Chapter 113 — The Forge
paragraphs: With matted beard, and wrapped in a bristling sharkskin apron, Perth was standing about midday between his forge and anvil, the anvil set on an ironwood log, with one hand holding a pike-head in the coals and the other at his forge's lungs, the bellows, when Captain Ahab came along, carrying in his hand a small, rusty-looking leather bag. While still a little distance from the forge, moody Ahab paused; until at last Perth, drawing his iron out of the fire, began hammering it on the anvil — the red mass sending off sparks in thick hovering flights, some of which flew close to Ahab.
"Are these your Mother Carey's chickens, Perth? They are always flying in your wake; birds of good omen, too, but not to all — look here, they burn; but you — you live among them without a scorch."
"Because I am scorched all over, Captain Ahab," answered Perth, resting for a moment on his hammer; "I am past scorching; not easily can you scorch a scar."

"Well, well; no more. Your shrunken voice sounds too calmly, sanely woeful to me. In no Paradise myself, I am impatient of all misery in others that is not mad. You should go mad, blacksmith; say, why don't you go mad? How can you endure without being mad? Do the heavens yet hate you, that you cannot go mad? What were you making there?"
"Welding an old pike-head, sir; there were seams and dents in it."
"And can you make it all smooth again, blacksmith, after such hard usage as it had?"
"I think so, sir."
"And I suppose you can smooth almost any seams and dents; never mind how hard the metal, blacksmith?"
"Aye, sir, I think I can; all seams and dents but one."

"Look here, then," cried Ahab, passionately advancing, and leaning with both hands on Perth's shoulders; "look here — here — can you smooth out a seam like this, blacksmith?" sweeping one hand across his furrowed brow; "if you could, blacksmith, I would gladly lay my head upon your anvil, and feel your heaviest hammer between my eyes. Answer! Can you smooth this seam?"
"Oh! That is the one, sir! Did I not say all seams and dents but one?"

"Aye, blacksmith, it is the one; aye, man, it is unsmoothable; for though you only see it here in my flesh, it has worked down into the bone of my skull — that is all wrinkles! But away with child's play; no more gaffs and pikes today. Look here!" jingling the leather bag as if it were full of gold coins. "I, too, want a harpoon made; one that a thousand yoke of fiends could not pull apart, Perth; something that will stick in a whale like his own fin-bone. There's the stuff," flinging the pouch upon the anvil. "Look, blacksmith, these are the gathered nail-stubs of the steel shoes of racing horses."
"Horseshoe stubs, sir? Why, Captain Ahab, you have here, then, the best and stubbornest stuff we blacksmiths ever work."

"I know it, old man. These stubs will weld together like glue made from the melted bones of murderers. Quick! Forge me the harpoon. First make me twelve rods for its shank; then wind and twist and hammer the twelve together like the yarns and strands of a towline. Quick! I'll blow the fire."

When at last the twelve rods were made, Ahab tried them, one by one, by spiraling them with his own hand round a long, heavy iron bolt. "A flaw!" rejecting the last one. "Work that over again, Perth."

When that was done, Perth was about to start welding the twelve into one, but Ahab stopped him and said he would weld his own iron. So Ahab hammered away on the anvil with steady, gasping grunts, while Perth handed him the glowing rods one after another and the hard-driven forge sent up its fierce, straight flame. Meanwhile the Parsee passed by without a word and, bowing over his head toward the fire, seemed to be calling down some curse or some blessing on the work. But when Ahab looked up, the Parsee slipped away to one side.

"What's that bunch of lucifer matches dodging about there for?" muttered Stubb, looking on from the forecastle. "That Parsee smells fire like a fuse; and smells of it himself, like a hot musket's powder-pan."
Finally the shank, now one complete rod, got its last heating; and when Perth plunged it, all hissing, into the nearby cask of water to temper it, the scalding steam shot up into Ahab's bent face.
"Would you brand me, Perth?" wincing for a moment with the pain; "have I been but forging my own branding-iron, then?"
"God forbid, not that; and yet I am afraid of something, Captain Ahab. Isn't this harpoon meant for the White Whale?"
"For the white fiend! But now for the barbs; you must make them yourself, man. Here are my razors — the best of steel; here, and make the barbs sharp as the needle-sleet of the Icy Sea."
For a moment the old blacksmith looked at the razors as if he would prefer not to use them.
"Take them, man, I have no need for them; for I now neither shave, eat, nor pray till — but here — to work!"

At last the steel was hammered into the shape of an arrowhead, and once Perth had welded it to the shank, it soon formed the point of the iron. As the blacksmith was about to give the barbs a final heating before tempering them, he called to Ahab to set the water-cask close by.

"No, no — no water for that; I want it of the true death-temper. Ahoy, there! Tashtego, Queequeg, Daggoo! What do you say, pagans! Will you give me as much blood as will cover this barb?" holding it high up. A cluster of dark nods replied: Yes. Three punctures were made in the heathen flesh, and the White Whale's barbs were then tempered.

"Ego non baptizo te in nomine patris, sed in nomine diaboli!" (I do not baptize you in the name of the father, but in the name of the devil!) deliriously howled Ahab, as the malignant iron scorchingly devoured the baptismal blood.

Next, Ahab gathered up the spare poles from below, picked one of hickory with the bark still on it, and fitted its end into the socket of the iron. Then a coil of new tow-line was unwound, and several fathoms of it were led to the windlass and pulled very taut. Ahab pressed his foot down on it until the rope hummed like a harp-string; then, bending eagerly over it and finding no broken strands, he exclaimed, "Good! Now for the seizings."

At one end the rope was unstranded, and the separate spread yarns were all braided and woven round the socket of the harpoon; the pole was then driven hard up into the socket; from the lower end the rope was traced halfway along the pole's length and firmly secured there with intertwistings of twine. This done, pole, iron and rope — like the Three Fates — remained inseparable, and Ahab moodily stalked away with the weapon, the sound of his ivory leg and the sound of the hickory pole both ringing hollowly along every plank. But before he entered his cabin, a light, unnatural, half-bantering, yet most piteous sound was heard. Oh, Pip! Your wretched laugh, your idle but unresting eye, all your strange mummery blended, not without meaning, with the black tragedy of the melancholy ship, and mocked it!
